note: Blocker scopes are joined, not summed. A Master Library source gap, a legal-design blocker and a mapping blocker are different questions about the same build and are counted separately; the joined unique count deduplicates by dedupeKey so one issue appearing in a state review and in the edition's gap ledger is counted once. No total here is hard-coded in application logic.

scopes.master_library_source_gap: Derived from MISSING_FILES_AND_SOURCE_GAPS.csv. The edition records the source as missing, unposted, unconfirmed or local-only.
scopes.legal_review_coverage_blocker: The adopted edition retains no controlling legal review for the jurisdiction. Counted once per jurisdiction.
scopes.legal_design_reconciliation_blocker: The controlling amended source and the current normalization disagree, or an expected source track ID has no express disposition. Failed closed rather than reconciled by rewriting the normalization.
scopes.legal_design_blocker: Derived from normalized track data. LegalEase cannot determine what to generate.
scopes.source_or_currentness_blocker: The source exists, but revision, currentness, provenance, licensing or official status remains open.
scopes.mapping_blocker: The source exists but is not mapped to the correct normalized track or packet unit under the adopted edition.
scopes.commercial_use_blocker: The publisher's licensing or commercial-use terms are unresolved.
scopes.source_acquisition_blocker: A required normalized-track source the edition does not manifest in a usable form. Counted once per document identity, not once per dependent component.
scopes.source_currentness_blocker: The document is identified, but the issuer's current revision could not be confirmed.
scopes.source_provenance_blocker: The issuing authority, retrieval provenance or statewide-versus-local status of a required source is unestablished.
scopes.technical_blocker: Field mapping, rendering, storage, access or completed-output proof is incomplete.
scopes.visual_or_legal_output_blocker: A rendered output has not passed legal and visual review.
scopes.jurisdiction_input_requirement: A priority county, court, district, circuit or local implementation has not been supplied.
scopes.runtime_promotion_blocker: Edition-wide: every retained asset is generation-disabled, so nothing can be promoted from the library alone.

The corpus holds no county prosecutor application, so the written-request branch is generated against the statute and the portal branch routes the participant to the county system.

The current revision status of EXP107. The copy held in the corpus is Rev 01/15 and no newer revision has been confirmed. The track is disabled for direct delivery, so this is a release matter rather than a legal-design blocker.
Whether § 609A.02, subd. 4 formally binds an inherent-authority order. The review treats the registration bar as excluded as a matter of policy.

The printed revision and current publication status of CR370, the Judgment and Order of Expungement under § 610.140. The form exists and is published by the Office of the State Courts Administrator — Missouri circuit clerks list it by number and title in their own form indexes — but courts.mo.gov returns HTTP 403 to automated retrieval from this environment, so no binary could be acquired and no revision stamp confirmed. Neither the repository corpus nor Master Library Edition 1.1 holds it; the repository's own artifact registry carries a CR370 row recorded as missing. The packet identity does not depend on it, but the proposed-order component cannot be field-mapped or rendered until the original is obtained.

Whether any Missouri circuit requires a locally drafted proposed judgment, or prepares the judgment itself under Rule 155.05, rather than accepting CR370 tendered with the petition. Missouri practice differs by circuit and the review left it unresolved whether any circuit rejects the statewide form in favour of a local one. The track carries localFormOverride and the proposed order is a conditional component for this reason.

The current standard circuit filing fee and cost schedule for a § 610.140 expungement case. County-variable and not published centrally. Rule 155.02 governs filing fees and costs but does not fix an amount. No fee figure is published on this track; the participant confirms with the clerk before filing.

Whether the current SJRC (10-24) CR360 remains the published revision as of the current date. The corpus copy is SJRC (10-24) and Master Library Edition 1.1 retains it as a packet-form candidate; the Missouri Courts expungement forms index reports its expungement form set as updated 1 January 2025, which is consistent with a form stamped 10-24 being published effective 1 January 2025 alongside the S.B. 754 amendments. Byte-level confirmation against the publisher could not be made because courts.mo.gov returns HTTP 403 to automated retrieval.

CR360 does not recite the § 610.140.13 lifetime caps anywhere on its face. The 2024 S.B. 754 limits — not more than three misdemeanor offenses or imprisonable ordinance violations, not more than two felony offenses, no limit on infractions — govern eligibility but appear only in paragraph 6's open-ended prior-expungement disclosure. The packet must carry the caps as an instruction; a participant working from the form alone would not learn of them.

How a participant with cases charged in more than one Missouri county obtains complete relief. § 610.140.2(2) requires every crime sought to be expunged to be listed in the one petition, while § 610.140.2(1) fixes venue by the court where the person was charged or found guilty; the two cannot both be satisfied across counties. The review records multi-county records as a referral trigger and the track treats it as a hard self-help stop rather than resolving it.

How an arrest-only § 610.140.7 petition should be presented on CR360, whose printed body text is written for convictions. The form says all of the convictions listed below occurred and were prosecuted within the state of Missouri and that the petition is filed in the county where the conviction was charged or the petitioner found guilty, both of which are wrong for an arrest with no charge filed in the arrest county. The Office of the State Courts Administrator publishes no separate arrest-only § 610.140 form. The packet supplies the § 610.140.7 allegations on a required continuation rather than altering the form's printed text, which is the fail-closed reading, but whether Missouri clerks accept that presentation is unconfirmed.

Whether the Case Types List's XG code, captioned Expungement of Crim/Arrest Record, is intended for a § 610.140.7 arrest-only petition rather than the X5 code captioned Expungement of Records (610.140 RSMo). The list is organised by statute, not by the word arrest, and X5 names § 610.140 expressly, so X5 is used and XG is reserved for the § 610.122 route. The caption of XG makes the point arguable and a misfiled case type is bounced at the counter.

Whether the § 610.140.13 lifetime caps count an arrest-only expungement granted under § 610.140.7, and if so at what offense level, given that subsection 13 counts misdemeanor offenses, imprisonable ordinance violations and felony offenses rather than arrests. An arrest that never became a charge has no conviction level. Unresolved on the face of the statute, and material because it decides whether using this route costs the participant a lifetime slot.

Whether closure under § 610.105 reaches arresting-agency records and central-repository entries, or only the records of the court in which the case originated. The section speaks of official records pertaining to the case becoming closed records, which is broad, and § 610.120 governs who may still see a closed record; but the section does not enumerate custodians and does not direct any agency to act. It determines what the participant should expect to see on a Highway Patrol record and on a background check, and the review left it open.

Whether Missouri provides any participant-facing mechanism to compel closure where § 610.105 closure did not take effect. None was located: the section creates no remedy, no Office of the State Courts Administrator form addresses it, and the Highway Patrol's record-review challenge procedure runs through the Patrol and back to the reporting agency rather than through a court. The track therefore retains pure guidance and refers the participant out rather than asserting a route. If counsel identifies a motion, application or written demand that does exist, this becomes a packet.

The current cost of a standard fingerprint card and whether every Missouri local law enforcement agency will produce one. A secondary Missouri pro se guide published in June 2024 records three dollars per card at one metropolitan police department, payable in cash, with a warning that some agencies cannot complete three cards in a visit. That is one agency in one region in one year and is not a statewide figure. The procedure is now known well enough to instruct a participant — a local law enforcement agency, three cards, ring ahead, bring identification — which is what the review's build blocker actually needed; the price is not.

Whether the current SJRC (04-24) CR145 remains the published revision as of the current date. Master Library Edition 1.1 retains it as a packet-form candidate and it supersedes the OSCA (10-16) copy the review examined. Byte-level confirmation against the publisher could not be made because courts.mo.gov returns HTTP 403 to automated retrieval.

How the § 610.124 blacking-out alternative is presented to a participant. The section requires destruction, and where destruction is not feasible because of the permanent nature of the record books the entries are blacked out instead. The packet cannot say which will happen to any particular record, and a participant told their record will be destroyed and then shown a redacted page will reasonably feel misled. The instructions state both outcomes; whether counsel wants a stronger caveat is open.

Two independent Missouri sources confirm no statewide form exists — the 16th Judicial Circuit's informational sheet says there are no forms provided and the applicant or their attorney must draft and file all pleadings, and a June 2024 pro se guide lists § 610.130 among the statutes with no Missouri court forms prepared. Local publication is not excluded and the track carries localFormOverride for that reason.

Which FI-05 case type code a § 610.130 application takes where a new case is opened. The official Case Types List publishes only XG, X5 and X# for expungement and none of them names this section. The code is left blank and confirmed with the clerk rather than guessed from a similar track name.

Who gives notice of the § 610.130 hearing, and to whom. The section requires a hearing but prescribes no notice recipients, no objection window and no service rule, unlike §§ 610.140.6 and 610.123.3 which do all three. Whether the clerk notices the prosecutor as on the § 610.140 routes, or the applicant serves the named respondents, is local practice. How a participant currently on probation or parole for a qualifying marijuana offense obtains the automatic vacatur and termination of supervision Article XIV gives them. The constitution says the sentence is vacated and supervision terminated without a petition, and CR375 offers no posture that fits them — its two boxes are currently incarcerated and not currently incarcerated or on probation. If supervision is in fact still running, the participant has a constitutional right nobody has enforced and no form to enforce it with. The unit 1 guidance describes the right and refers to counsel; it does not manufacture a motion.

Whether the Office of the State Courts Administrator publishes a numbered proposed order or certificate of expungement for the Article XIV route. None could be located, and courts.mo.gov returns HTTP 403 to automated retrieval from this environment so the forms index could not be read directly. How a participant verifies that automatic or court-ordered Article XIV expungement already occurred, where Case.net and the Highway Patrol record disagree or are both silent. A case that vanishes from Case.net may have been expunged, may never have been on Case.net, or may sit in a municipal division Case.net does not cover. Which FI-05 case type code a § 610.145 petition takes, and whether a cover sheet is required at all where the petition proceeds under the original case number. How the § 610.145.3 fee exemption is claimed in practice where a court requires an opening fee to commence a new case. The review left this open and it remains open.

Whether a participant may invoke § 610.145.1(2) where the prosecutor or judicial officer who ordered the dismissal did not give the required notice. What a substantial number of identifying factors means in practice under § 575.120.4. The section supplies the standard but no gloss, and Missouri case law construing it was not located on this pass. It matters because it is the whole merits of the petition: a participant whose name alone was used may not meet it, while one whose name, date of birth and Social Security number were all ascribed plainly does. The packet lists what the participant says was used and does not characterise it.

Which FI-05 case type code a § 575.120.4 correction petition takes. The published Case Types List names no code for it, and its XG code is captioned Expungement of Crim/Arrest Record, which describes the § 610.122 route rather than a correction. A June 2024 Missouri pro se guide reports X1, Other Miscellaneous Action, in the circuit column, for identity-theft filings. The code is left blank and confirmed with the clerk.

Whether § 610.124's destruction regime applies to a correction ordered under § 575.120.4. § 575.120.4 borrows the procedures set forth in § 610.123, and § 610.124 by its terms governs all records ordered to be expunged pursuant to § 610.123. On that reading the false identifying factors would be destroyed or blacked out and removed from Missouri electronic files, with the central repository requesting Federal Bureau of Investigation expungement. That is a strong reading with real participant consequences and the packet does not assert it: it says the false factors are corrected and expunged, and does not promise destruction.

Whether any Missouri circuit, associate or municipal division publishes a local form for a § 311.326 expungement, notwithstanding that the Office of the State Courts Administrator publishes none. A June 2024 Missouri pro se guide lists § 311.326 among the statutes for which no Missouri court forms are prepared and directs the reader to draft their own petition. Local publication is not excluded and the track carries localFormOverride for that reason.

Whether § 311.326 requires a hearing. The section says that if the court determines, upon review, that the conditions are met, the court shall enter an order of expungement — upon review rather than after hearing, which is the wording § 610.130.2 uses. On its face no hearing is required, which would make this the only Missouri petition route without one, but the section does not forbid one and Missouri courts may set one as a matter of practice. The packet tells the participant to ask the clerk rather than promising either way.
Which FI-05 case type code a § 311.326 application takes where a new case is opened. The published Case Types List names no code for the section. The code is left blank and confirmed with the clerk.

Whether a conviction under a municipal or county underage-possession ordinance, rather than under § 311.325 itself, is within § 311.326. The section names the statute and the packet applies the narrower reading, which excludes ordinance convictions; but many Missouri underage-drinking cases are charged municipally, so the narrower reading takes a substantial population out of the route. Unresolved on the face of the section.

Whether § 610.141 is yet operating. Subsection 10 makes the section effective when technically feasible for both the Office of the State Courts Administrator and the central repository, but no later than 1 January 2027. Neither body has published an implementation notice, eligibility instructions, a form, a portal, a schedule or verification guidance that could be located, and the Highway Patrol's Criminal Records and Identification Division pages say nothing about automatic expungement, clean slate or § 610.141. The mechanism is enacted; it is not shown to be operating. The adopted memorandum makes an administering-agency implementation notice a condition of releasing this route, and that condition is not met.

The precise general effective date of § 610.141 as an enactment, as distinct from the operational trigger in subsection 10. CCS SS SB 1421 carries an emergency clause at Section B, but it applies only to the enactment of §§ 589.900 and 589.902 and the repeal and reenactment of § 577.800, and there is no general effective-date section. The remaining sections therefore take effect on the ordinary Missouri constitutional date for an act of a session that adjourned on 15 May 2026, which is 28 August 2026. The distinction matters because subsection 10 then conditions the section's provisions on technical feasibility with a 1 January 2027 outer limit, so enactment, effectiveness and operation are three different dates and the participant-facing statement must use the right one.

How a participant learns that an automatic expungement has occurred. The section provides no notice to the person whose record is expunged: the repository notifies the Supreme Court and the Office of the State Courts Administrator, and § 610.141.12's explanatory document is given at sentencing or on release from supervision rather than when relief arrives. The only practical check is a fingerprint-based Highway Patrol record the participant pays for. That is a real gap in a scheme whose whole premise is that people should not have to act.

How the § 610.141.6 shared cap operates in time. The subsection limits an offender to three misdemeanor and two felony expungements under § 610.141 and § 610.140 combined, and § 610.140.13 as it stands counts only expungements granted under § 610.140. Whether a § 610.140 petition granted before § 610.141 becomes operative counts against the combined limit, and whether the repository can see prior § 610.140 expungements when it runs its analysis, are not addressed. It matters directly: a participant with two prior § 610.140 felony expungements may or may not be within the combined felony cap.

Whether the § 610.143 consumer-reporting and employer-immunity provisions apply to expungements granted under § 610.140 as well as under § 610.141. § 610.143 speaks generally of records for which a full pardon or expungement has been granted, and sits between the two, but is enacted in the same act as the automatic mechanism. If it reaches § 610.140 orders it is a substantial and previously unavailable participant-facing benefit that belongs in the § 610.140 packet instructions as well, and the packet does not currently assert it there.

Whether the Miss. Code Ann. § 99-19-72 fee reaches a given petition. The section reads: 'A filing fee of One Hundred Fifty Dollars ($150.00) is hereby levied on each petition to expunge an offense under Section 99-19-71 to be collected by the circuit clerk', distributed $100 to the Judicial System Operation Fund, $40 to the District Attorneys Operation Fund and $10 retained by the circuit clerk. Last amended by Laws, 1st Ex. Sess. 2017, ch. 7, § 12; no enacted amendment through 2026. Two things remain unresolved on its face and are NOT resolved by construction here. First, the trigger is 'each petition to expunge AN OFFENSE under Section 99-19-71': a § 99-19-71(4) non-conviction petition is a petition under § 99-19-71 but is not a petition to expunge an offence, because there is no conviction, and the statute does not settle it either way. Second, the collection mechanism names the CIRCUIT CLERK, which does not map onto § 99-19-71(1) or (4) petitions filed in justice or municipal court. Sections 9-11-15(3), 21-23-7(6), 99-15-26, 63-11-30, 41-29-150 and 67-3-70 sit outside § 99-19-71 and the fee does not reach them by its terms; none of those sections specifies a fee of its own. The packet therefore publishes NO fee amount on any track and instructs the participant to confirm the filing fee, and any pauper's-affidavit route, with the clerk of the court before filing.

Local practice in the twenty-one circuit court districts other than the Fourth, and in every municipal and justice court, was not surveyed. Both the review and the Fourth District materials establish that districts maintain their own petition and order preferences and that some expect the district attorney to sign the order as approved as to form before the judge will sign. This is a scaling constraint rather than a legal one: the statutory mechanism is the same statewide, but the accepted document and the practical gate vary. Every Mississippi track therefore carries localFormOverride and a mandatory clerk-contact instruction.

Trafficking-survivor relief under Miss. Code Ann. § 97-3-54.6, as amended by 2026 HB 1546 effective 1 July 2026, is recorded here as a separately-listed matter and NOT as a tenth normalized source node, because neither the adopted Batch 2 memorandum nor the authoritative source crosswalk lists it among Mississippi's nine core adult slots. The enrolled text was read: new § 97-3-54.6(6) lets the sentencing court, at any time after a conviction or adjudication of delinquency of a misdemeanour or a felony not classified as a crime of violence under § 97-3-2, expunge on appropriate motion where it finds by a preponderance that participation in the offence occurred during the period the person was being trafficked and was the direct result of that trafficking; official documentation from a federal, state or local government agency creates a presumption but is not required; and new § 97-3-54.6(7)(b) provides that neither failing to raise the trafficking affirmative defence nor the court's finding on it affects the ability to file under subsection (6). This relief is broader and faster than ordinary § 99-19-71 conviction expungement, so screening for it belongs on every intake. Whether it becomes a normalized node requires an express crosswalk or memorandum instruction.

Whether a case 'passed to the file' or 'retired to the file' counts as a case in which there was 'no disposition' under § 99-19-71(4). Mississippi practice uses that phrasing and the statute does not address it. The packet fails closed: the participant is asked to copy the docket wording, and an ambiguous entry routes to advice rather than to a pleaded allegation.

Whether the ten days' written notice to the district attorney required by § 99-19-71(2)(b) applies outside the felony conviction subsection. On the enrolled text the requirement sits inside subsection (2), which governs felony conviction expungement, and subsection (4) contains no notice provision. The packet does not import the felony notice rule, and instead serves the prosecuting authority contemporaneously and tells the participant that local practice may expect more.
